idiom_name: key -> builder map (registry table) + register step + create(key) lookup
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one associative table from key to builder, a registration step that is filled where the implementations live (a configuration function, module init, or a per-type registration hook), and one create(key) that resolves the key, calls the builder and returns the product typed as the abstraction. Keep the table private to the kit; make the product type in the builder signature the abstract one; decide explicitly what a duplicate key and an unknown key do (error is the safer default) and whether registration closes after startup. Where the language has no first-class functions, the same table holds function pointers or creator objects, and where it has no lazy statics the table is filled from an explicit init function. This table replaces the classic one-factory-subclass-per-family structure; that structure remains justified only when creation is fixed at compile time and must be checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: Forgetting the registration step for one product turns into a create-time error only when that key is first used — test that every advertised key can actually be created.
A kit that hands out constructed instances rather than builders stops being a factory and becomes a registry of singletons, discarding per-call construction.
Keys that come from outside the program name any registered implementation — validate them against the table and never pass them further (class loading, file paths, untrusted network input).

Shared mutable state without thread safety: if the registry is written from one thread and read from another (or written concurrently), data races cause crash or silent corruption; freeze the table after configuration.

Cross-module key hashing: in languages like Swift with whole-module optimization, keys stored as StaticString may be hashed by pointer address, causing identical strings registered in different modules to produce different hashes at runtime — use content-based hashing for cross-module keys.

Registration order dependencies: when builder A needs builder B to already be registered, load order silently changes behaviour; document registration dependencies and validate them in a startup integration test.

Drifting into a service locator: as caching, scoping, and contextual resolution are added, the kit becomes a general service locator and the create call becomes the only coupling surface — keep the scope of the kit intentionally narrow.

Wrong move: relying on import-time self-registration (decorators, static initializers, __init_subclass__) -> a product whose module was never imported is silently missing and create() dies with an 'unknown key' error far from the registration site, and load order silently changes behaviour -> register through an explicit init list or config function the entry point calls, and test every advertised key can be created.

Wrong move: storing constructed instances in the table to skip builder boilerplate -> the process pins every product ever registered, captured closures force eager construction, and in multiprocessing workers the registration state (pickled closures, globals) is missing or diverges -> store builder functions that construct on demand.

Wrong move: one global register(string, fn) written from arbitrary module-level code -> a duplicate key silently overwrites another module's builder and behaviour depends on import order -> make the table private to the kit, error on duplicates, and freeze it once the configuration phase ends.
